newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EMU wannabes should mull going Dutch - economists.
newsitem.headline: EMU wannabes should mull going Dutch - economists.

text.p: Countries aspiring to qualify for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would do well to take note of the Netherlands, economists say.

Dutch policy makers know how to operate in an EMU environment. The guilder has been tightly pegged to the mark for 15 years, and as its 1997 budget showed, the Netherlands has economic credentials which are the envy of Europe, they say.
The key to the textbook Dutch economic performance -- 2.5 percent GDP growth, inflation of 2.25 percent, and falling unemployment -- is the unrelenting drive to stay competitive.

With its quasi-fixed exchange rate policy, the option of tinkering with the value of the guilder to achieve international competitiveness has long been ruled out. So policymakers rely on low wage inflation and productivity improvements.
Economists say the Dutch case highlights that real improvements in competiveness are an essential partner to fixed exchange rates.

"It's very important to realise that just fixing exchange rates is not enough," said Wike Groenenberg of Salomon Brothers in London. "The fact it's worked in the Dutch case...is because of the internal policies to ensure the link is maintained."

Christer Lindholm, economist at J.P. Morgan, agreed. "Regardless of whether Germany is your main trading partner, most European countries -- France in particular is suffering from some competitiveness problems at present -- can take lessons from (the Dutch experience)," he said.
The guilder was last devalued against the mark in 1983. At present it may officially move within a 2.25 percent band around the German currency, but in practice, the link is far stronger.
The consensus wage bargaining tradition of the Netherlands is key to its low wage inflation, as is its flexible work force.

Union acceptance of a jobs over pay principle and laws which make hiring part-time and temporary workers easy have kept wages in check and put more people back to work, thus driving down the government deficit and reducing pressure on the welfare system.

As the Dutch prepare to take over the presidency of the European Union in January, they do so with almost 15 years of competitive improvements behind them. The results were evident in the 1997 Dutch budget, presented to parliament last week.
The government's Central Planning Bureau forecast an inflation rate of 2.5 percent in 1997, just 25 basis points above the EU average and so comfortably within EMU criteria.
The deficit was forecast at 2.25 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), within the 3.0 percent EMU limit and well below the 3.5 percent EU average.
Economic growth was expected to reach 2.75 percent in 1997, private consumption was seen growing by 1.75 percent and unemployment falling to 5.25 percent from 6.0 percent in 1996.
So as European neighbours slash debt and muzzle inflation in a race to meet stringent EMU standards can they expect to match the Netherlands' economic success and social harmony?

Paribas economist Stefan Schneider said the Dutch success story is explained in part by close economic ties with Germany which absorbs a third of Dutch exports but also by its staunchly independent central bank, something else it shares with Germany.
"The ultimate reason is that both countries have central banks that have earned their credibility," he added.
This has insulated the guilder from speculative attacks that have shaken less solid European currencies.
Schneider questioned whether other European countries had the social consensus necessary to implement sweeping labour reforms and mirror the Dutch experience.
Lindholm warned that adopting the Dutch approach to competitiveness improvements would not prove a quick fix but could deliver in the longer term.
"This kind of policy doesn't produce immediate benefits... But beyond 1999 it would definitely be sensible (for EMU countries) to try to achieve something like this."
